title: Oblates
hook: laypeople who follow the spirit of the Rule in ordinary life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the family of Benedict: Cluny, the Cistercians, the Trappists. Your line was one rule, many houses. Did you meet a branch, not a break? Day one thousand two hundred six.

A nurse finishing a night shift. A retired mechanic. A mother of three who keeps a worn copy of the Rule in the glove compartment. None of them lives in a monastery. None of them wears a habit. But each of them belongs, in a real way, to one particular abbey, and tries to live by Benedict's Rule in a house with a mortgage and a washing machine. The family of Benedict has a branch that doesn't live behind any wall at all. Today's word: oblate.
screen: `A NURSE, A MECHANIC, A MOTHER.` → `NO HABIT, NO CLOISTER.` → `BENEDICT'S RULE AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Oblate means one who is offered. The language goes back to the Rule itself. In chapter fifty-nine, Benedict describes parents who offer a son to the monastery. They wrap the boy's hand, together with their written promise, in the cloth of the altar, and so give him to God. That custom of offering children ended long ago. But the word stayed, and it came to name something new: men and women outside the cloister, single or married, who offer their lives to God in the spirit of the Rule while staying exactly where they are. Here's how it works today. An oblate attaches to one particular monastery, usually after a time of getting to know it. Then, in a short ceremony, they make an oblation: a promise to live by the spirit of the Rule as their life allows. It's a promise, not the vows of a monk. They don't move in. They don't give up their homes or their marriages. What they take home is the shape of the life. Some of the psalms and prayers the monks pray, at morning or evening. A daily time of slow reading with Scripture. Work done carefully, as if the tools were altar vessels. Guests received as Christ. And a link to their monastery, which prays for them and which they visit when they can. Go back to stability, the first of the three vows. A monk stays with one community. An oblate stays too, in a different way: tied to one house, carrying its rhythm into a kitchen, a classroom, a hospital ward. The Rule was written for people behind walls. Oblates show that it fits through a front door.
screen: `ONE WHO IS OFFERED.` · `A PROMISE, NOT A MONK'S VOWS.` · `PSALMS, READING, WORK, GUESTS.` · then, large: `THE RULE AT HOME.` · then: `TIED TO ONE MONASTERY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your nearest monastery. Not now, on your phone. Later, if you want to. For now, settle and breathe. Let yourself wonder where the closest community of monks or nuns might be: a hill outside town, a city block, a farm road. Picture its bell ringing for prayer while you sit here. You and they share this hour. If you pray, you can pray with them, wherever they are. If not, just keep the quiet alongside them. The bell holds the time.
Oblate. One who is offered: a layperson tied to a Benedictine monastery, living the spirit of the Rule in ordinary life. Today's word.

Your line: the rule at home. Today, take one piece of the Rule's chapters into your own house: a guest treated like Christ, a tool handled with care, a few minutes of reading. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: Benedictine oblates attach themselves to a particular monastery, make an oblation after a period of preparation, and try to live the spirit of the Rule at home through daily prayer, spiritual reading and work.

original.note: Latin: offered, the sense behind the English word oblate.

trapdoor: what you thought: only monks and nuns live by Benedict's Rule.
what it means: oblates are laypeople tied to one monastery, living the spirit of the Rule at home.
what a scholar hears: the name recalls chapter fifty-nine, where parents offered a child to the monastery wrapped in the altar cloth.

notes: 'Oblate means one who is offered' and the Latin 'oblatus': a word origin, stated plainly. The Rule's ch. 59 speaks of children who are offered (offeruntur); please confirm the connection is phrased acceptably.
Ch. 59 summary: parents write the petition, wrap it and the child's hand in the altar cloth, and offer him. Confirm.
'That custom of offering children ended long ago' has no date by design; confirm.

Modern oblate practice (attachment to one monastery, a period of preparation, oblation as a promise not vows, single or married, some of the Office, lectio divina) is described generally; customs vary by monastery. Confirm wording, and whether clergy should also be mentioned.
The hook's nurse, mechanic and mother are illustrative, not real people.
Editor pass: carry no longer says 'this week's chapters' (the Rule chapters ran across more than a week).
